## 7 Some implications of factorized solutions

### 7.1 Spin-glass-like metastable states

As we discussed in the section 5, we can use the extended reparametrization symmetry (79),(80) to generate more physically interesting solutions from a factorized solution. For example, we can make the time dependence of replica-offdiagonal components of the field $G_{\alpha\beta}$ differ from the time dependence of the diagonal components if we act with the set of diffeomorphisms $V_{\alpha}\in\text{diff}(S^{1})$ which is arranged in such a way that

$$ \forall\alpha,\beta:\ \alpha\neq\beta\,,\;V_{\alpha}=V_{\beta}\circ U_{\beta},\ \text{where}\ U_{\beta}\in SL(2,\mathbb{R})\,. $$

In this case all diagonal components will have the same time dependence, whereas the time dependence of the off-diagonal components will be different, because of the extra $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ transformation which acts only on one of the times.

#### Example.

Let us fix $M=2$ . We will work in terms of dimensionless times on the thermal circle

$$ \theta_{1,2}=\frac{2\pi}{\beta}\tau_{1,2}\,. $$

Consider the following pair of diffeomorphisms, where the first transformation is identity and the second one is a fraction linear transformation on the circle:

$$ \displaystyle\theta\to\varphi_{1}(\theta)=\theta\,; \displaystyle\theta\to\varphi_{2}(\theta)\,:\ \mathrm{e}^{i\varphi_{2}(\theta)}=\frac{a\mathrm{e}^{i\theta}+b}{c\mathrm{e}^{i\theta}+d}\,,\ ad-bc=1\,. $$

In this case the diagonal components $G_{11}$ and $G_{22}$ are invariant under these transformations and are given by

$$ G_{11}=g(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})P_{11}\,;\quad G_{22}=g(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})P_{22}\,. $$

However, the off-diagonal part transforms non-trivially:

$$ G_{12}\to\text{const}(d+c\ \mathrm{e}^{i\theta_{2}})^{-2\Delta}\left|\mathrm{e}^{i\theta_{1}}-\frac{a\mathrm{e}^{i\theta_{2}}+b}{c\mathrm{e}^{i\theta_{2}}+d}\right|^{-2\Delta}P_{12}\,. $$

In order to analyze the dependence on real time, we set $\theta_{1}=0$ and $\mathrm{e}^{i\theta_{2}}=e^{\frac{2\pi}{\beta}t_{2}}$ . Then, we obtain

$$ G_{12}(0,t_{2})\sim\left(d-b-(a-c)\mathrm{e}^{\frac{2\pi}{\beta}t_{2}}\right)^{-2\Delta}\,. $$

This is the decay law of the off-diagonal component. The exponent does not dominate until the characteristic time scale of

$$ t_{2}^{*}=\frac{\beta}{2\pi}\log\frac{d-b-1}{a-c}\,. $$

Since the $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ is non-compact, by fine tuning the parameters of the Möbius transformation, we can make this time scale as long as we like, so that

$$ \log\frac{d-b-1}{a-c}\gg 0\,. $$

For comparison, the diagonal components behave like

$$ G_{11}(0,t_{2})\sim(1-\mathrm{e}^{\frac{2\pi}{\beta}t_{2}})^{-2\Delta}\,, $$

and it starts decaying right away. This means that at short times $t_{2}<t_{2}^{*}$ the transformed solution is frozen, behaving like a kind of spin glass. However, after $t_{2}^{*}$ the thermal fluctuations destroy the spin-glass-like configuration with the same speed as a regular replica-diagonal configuration.

### 7.2 On relation to thermofield double and AdS2 gravity

#### 7.2.1 Thermofield double from two replicas

The emergent (extended) conformal invariance suggests that the factorized solutions might have a holographic interpretation in terms of nearly AdS2 gravity, like the replica-diagonal solution does [9, 11, 25]. The purpose of this section is to explore this correspondence on a toy example of factorized solution for $M=2$ .

In this case we need to solve the equation (84) for the $q=4$ and $M=2$ . Assuming the replica-symmetric form for $P$ like in (5.6.1), we arrive at the equations (141)-(142) with $M=2$ and $q=4$ :

$$ \displaystyle aA^{3}+Aa^{3} \displaystyle= \displaystyle 0\,; \displaystyle a^{4}+A^{4} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathcal{C}\,. $$

Fixing the scaling with $a=1$ , we arrive at the solution with

$$ \displaystyle P_{11}=P_{22}\equiv a=1\,;\qquad P_{12}=P_{21}\equiv A=i\,; \displaystyle\mathcal{C}=2\,. $$

We now apply a pair of reparametrizations to the solution using (79):

$$ f_{1}(\tau)=\tau\,;\qquad f_{2}(\tau)=\tau+\frac{\beta}{2}\,. $$

Each of these transformations belongs to $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ , so diagonal elements of $G$ are unchanged, whereas the off-diagonal elements transform non-trivially. The transformed solution is given by

$$ \displaystyle G_{11}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})=G_{22}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})=\frac{b}{2^{\Delta}}\left(\frac{\pi}{\beta J}\right)^{2\Delta}\frac{\text{sgn}(\tau_{1}-\tau_{2})}{\left|\sin\frac{\pi}{\beta}(\tau_{1}-\tau_{2})\right|^{2\Delta}}\,; \displaystyle G_{12}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})=G_{21}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})=\frac{b}{2^{\Delta}}\left(\frac{\pi}{\beta J}\right)^{2\Delta}\frac{i\ \text{sgn}(\tau_{1}-\tau_{2})}{\left|\cos\frac{\pi}{\beta}(\tau_{1}-\tau_{2})\right|^{2\Delta}}\,. $$

When performing the analytic continuation to the Lorentzian signature, it is evident that (216),(217) are, correspondingly, one-sided and two-sided correlators of a Majorana fermion in the thermofield double state [36, 37, 25]. The transformations (215) make it explicit that the two-sided (off-diagonal) correlator can be obtained from a one-sided (diagonal) correlator by moving one of the endpoints halfway along the thermal circle [37]. Thus, a replica-nondiagonal large $N$ saddle point of the SYK model with $M=2$ replicas in the conformal limit can describe the purification of a single replica of SYK model at finite temperature in the form of the thermofield double state.

#### 7.2.2 Comparison with semiclassical holographic computation

We can compare the factorized solution (216),(217) with what we can get from a holographic computation of correlators in the AdS2 spacetime. We consider the Lorentzian AdS2 spacetime, which is described in embedding space of signature $(-\ -\ +)$ as a hyperboloid defined by the equation [9, 25]

$$ -T_{1}^{2}-T_{2}^{2}+X^{2}=-1\,. $$

We are interested in the Schwarzschild coordinate patch in the AdS2. Let us denote by symbols $L$ and $R$ two boundaries of the AdS2. In this case there are two corresponding choices of the Schwarzshild patch, which are described by the parametrizations [25]:

$$ \displaystyle T_{1}^{L}=\frac{r}{R}\,;\quad T_{1}^{R}=-\frac{r}{R}\,; \displaystyle T_{2}^{L,R}=\sqrt{\frac{r^{2}}{R^{2}}-1}\sinh Rt\,; \displaystyle X^{L,R}=\sqrt{\frac{r^{2}}{R^{2}}-1}\sinh Rt\,. $$

Here $r,t\in\mathbb{R}$ . The horizon radius is related to the temperature as $R=\frac{\pi}{\beta}$ . The induced metric in both cases is the same,

$$ ds^{2}=-(r^{2}-R^{2})dt^{2}+\frac{dr^{2}}{r^{2}-R^{2}}\,. $$

Suppose we want to calculate a correlator of heavy (scalar) operator $\mathcal{O}$ of the dimension $\Delta_{\mathcal{O}}$ inserted on the same boundary. In the limit $\Delta_{\mathcal{O}}\gg 1$ , the correlator is determined1010 10 In this discussion we do not go into the details about analytic continuations and $i\epsilon$ -prescription for correlators. We note that one can restore the analytic structure of the geodesic correlators by modifying the prescription to include the specific phase factors [39]. by the length $\mathcal{L}$ of the geodesic anchored on the boundary endpoints:

$$ G_{\Delta_{\mathcal{O}}}(t_{1},t_{2})\sim\mathrm{e}^{-\Delta_{\mathcal{O}}\mathcal{L}(t_{1},t_{2})} $$

Thus we need the boundary-to-boundary geodesics. The one-sided geodesics give complex-valued lengths because the interval is timelike, but we can circumvent this by making analytic continuation to the Euclidean signature $\tau=it$ in the parametrization and $T_{2}\to iT_{2}$ in the embedding space. To find the geodesic length between the points $1$ and $2$ , we can use the relation

$$ \cosh\mathcal{L}(1,2)=\langle\vec{Y}(1),\vec{Y}(2)\rangle\,, $$

where $\vec{Y}$ denotes a point in the embedding space, and angular brackets denote the scalar product in the embedding space. We choose the endpoints on the boundary, i. e. so that $r_{1}=r_{2}=r_{0}\to\infty$ . Taking the asymptotic with respect to $r_{0}$ and subtracting the divergent part, we obtain for one-sided correlator

$$ G_{\Delta_{\mathcal{O}}}^{LL}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\sim\left(\frac{1}{2\sin\frac{\pi}{\beta}(\tau_{1}-\tau_{2})}\right)^{\Delta_{\mathcal{O}}}\,, $$

and for the two-sided correlator

$$ G_{\Delta_{\mathcal{O}}}^{LR}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\sim\left(\frac{1}{2\cos\frac{\pi}{\beta}(\tau_{1}-\tau_{2})}\right)^{\Delta_{\mathcal{O}}}\,. $$

We see that the time dependence of these semiclassical correlators is captured properly by the $2$ -replica result (216),(217). However, it is clear that the structure of the Parisi matrix $P$ will not be captured by the bulk theory on the leading semiclassical level.

In conclusion to this remark we would like to note that in the holographic derivation we performed the analytic continuation to the Euclidean signature while trating it purely formally. It seems plausible that the actual bulk spacetime which would have to correspond to our analytically continued Lorentzian AdS2 would be similar to the double cone construction, described by authors of [26].

### 7.3 Comments on solutions beyond the strong coupling limit

#### 7.3.1 (In)applicability of separation of variables

Now let us make some comments about possible continuation of the factorized solutions (81) beyond the strong coupling regime. The non-conformal saddle point equation under the assumption of separability of variables (81) reads

$$ P_{\alpha\gamma}(\partial_{\tau}g)(\tau,\tau^{\prime\prime})-J^{2}\int d\tau^{\prime}g(\tau,\tau^{\prime})g(\tau^{\prime},\tau^{\prime\prime})^{q-1}P_{\alpha\beta}P_{\beta\gamma}^{q-1}=-\delta_{\alpha\gamma}\delta(\tau-\tau^{\prime\prime})\,. $$

Taking the diagonal and off-diagonal part, one can write

$$ \displaystyle P_{\alpha\alpha}(\partial_{\tau}g)(\tau,\tau^{\prime\prime})-J^{2}\int d\tau^{\prime}g(\tau,\tau^{\prime})g(\tau^{\prime},\tau^{\prime\prime})^{q-1}\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}=-\delta(\tau-\tau^{\prime\prime})\,; \displaystyle P_{\alpha\gamma}(\partial_{\tau}g)(\tau,\tau^{\prime\prime})-J^{2}\int d\tau^{\prime}g(\tau,\tau^{\prime})g(\tau^{\prime},\tau^{\prime\prime})^{q-1}P_{\alpha\beta}P_{\beta\gamma}^{q-1}=0\,,\quad\alpha\neq\gamma\,. $$

On the Parisi ansatz we have $P_{\alpha\alpha}=a_{0}$ , so $\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}=\mathcal{C}$ remains true beyond the conformal limit.

However, the ansatz in the form (81) is inconsistent with the full saddle point equation (227). Let us assume without loss of generality1111 11 The Parisi form assumption here is mainly for streamlining the notations. The statement is true for a generic matrix $P$ with properties $P_{\alpha\alpha}=a_{0}$ and $\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}=\mathcal{C}$ . that $P$ is a Parisi matrix, which can be represented using (255):

$$ P=\sum_{i}a_{i}(\mathcal{I}_{m_{i+1}}-\mathcal{I}_{m_{i}})+a_{0}I_{M}\,, $$

and that we fixed the scaling freedom by setting $\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}=\mathcal{C}=1$ . In this case the equation (228) can be written in operator form as

$$ a_{0}\partial_{\tau}\hat{g}-J^{2}\hat{g}*\hat{g}^{\circ(q-1)}=\bf{1}\,, $$

where $\bf{1}$ denotes the delta-function. To rewrite the the off-diagonal equation (229) in the convenient form, we introduce the Parisi matrix $Q$ :

$$ Q:=P\cdot P^{\circ(q-1)}=\sum_{i}w_{i}(\mathcal{I}_{m_{i+1}}-\mathcal{I}_{m_{i}})+w_{0}I_{M}\,. $$

Now we can expand the entire (229) in terms of the Parisi algebra generators and rewrite it in terms of the components:

$$ a_{i}\partial_{\tau}\hat{g}-J^{2}w_{i}\hat{g}*\hat{g}^{\circ(q-1)}=0\,. $$

We can extract the derivative term from (231) and substitute it into (233), which yields the equation

$$ J^{2}\hat{g}*\hat{g}^{\circ(q-1)}=-\left(1-\frac{w_{i}}{a_{i}}a_{0}\right)^{-1}{\bf 1}\,. $$

This equation says that the function $g(\tau,\tau^{\prime})$ is a conformal correlator, up to a constant factor. However, this contradicts the diagonal equation (231). This means that there are no exact saddles which have the factorized form, and we have to break an assumption e.g. about the time independence of $P$ . To find the exact UV completion of a factorized solution, we have to modify the factorized ansatz. One can show that this modification must be replica-nondiagonal.

#### 7.3.2 Strong coupling expansion

One would like to look for solutions of the equations (8),(9), which we will write in the operator form as

$$ \displaystyle\kappa\partial_{\tau}\hat{G}_{\alpha\gamma}-\sum_{\beta}\hat{G}_{\alpha\beta}*\hat{\Sigma}_{\beta\gamma} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\bf{1}\times\delta_{\alpha\gamma}\,; \displaystyle\hat{\Sigma}_{\alpha\beta} \displaystyle= \displaystyle J^{2}\hat{G}_{\alpha\beta}^{\circ(q-1)}\,. $$

Based on the above considerations, one has to look for the solution in the form

$$ G_{\alpha\beta}(\tau,\tau^{\prime})=g(\tau,\tau^{\prime})P_{\alpha\beta}+\Phi_{\alpha\beta}(\tau,\tau^{\prime})\,. $$

Perturbatively, the solution can be constructed using the strong coupling expansion in $\kappa$ :

$$ \Phi_{\alpha\beta}=\kappa\varphi_{\alpha\beta}^{(1)}+\kappa^{2}\varphi_{\alpha\beta}^{(2)}+\dots\,. $$

In the position space, the $\Sigma$ is then expanded as follows:

$$ \Sigma_{\alpha\beta}=g^{q-1}P_{\alpha\beta}^{q-1}+\kappa(q-1)J^{2}g^{q-2}P_{\alpha\beta}^{q-2}\varphi_{\alpha\beta}^{(1)}+\dots\,. $$

Next we substitute the expansions into (236) and equate the powers in $\kappa$ to $0$ . The $\kappa^{0}$ equation gives us the saddle point equations for the factorized configurations in the IR limit (85),(84). They are solved by $g$ given by (86) and a Parisi matrix $P$ .

The $\kappa^{1}$ equation reads

$$ \frac{1}{J^{2}}P_{\alpha\gamma}\partial_{\tau}\hat{g}=\sum_{\beta}\left[\hat{\varphi}_{\alpha\beta}^{(1)}*\hat{g}^{\circ(q-1)}P_{\beta\gamma}^{q-1}+(q-1)P_{\alpha\beta}\hat{g}*(\hat{g}^{\circ(q-2)}\hat{\varphi}_{\beta\gamma}^{(1)})P_{\beta\gamma}^{q-2}\right]\,. $$

This is again a linear inhomogeneous integral equation for $\hat{\varphi}_{\beta\gamma}^{(1)}$ . It is not very tractable analytically in general, but one can make some remarks:

- • If $P=I$ , then the equation (240) and equations for higher degrees of $\kappa$ ensure that $\Phi_{\alpha\beta}=0$ for $\alpha\neq\beta$ , as can be expected from general intuition and known numerical solutions of exact saddle point equations in the replica-diagonal case (see e.g. [3]).

- • The replica dependence in the equation (240) would mean that if one was to take the replica limit $M\to 0$ like we do in the strong coupling limit in section 5, this will mean that one would arrive at the integral equation for a function $\varphi(\tau,\tau^{\prime};u)$ of three variables, with mixed integrals in time and replica variables.

First, we have studied the exact nondiagonal saddles, analytically in the $q=2$ model and numerically in the $q=4$ model.

- 1. For $q=2$ we found exact analytic replica-nondiagonal solutions of the saddle point equations, given by the formulae (43)-(46), for arbitrary $M>0$ . As we have discussed, these solutions are singular in the limit $M\to 0$ . It is easy to check that the on-shell action in the zero replica limit is also singular, which means that there is no well-defined limit of zero replicas on this class of solutions. Another significant property of these solutions is the non-analyticity in coupling constant at $J=0$ . This confirms the nonperturbative nature of the nondiagonal solutions, discussed in the section 2.2.

- 2. Our numerical study shows that for every exact $q=2$ nondiagonal solution there is a numerical real-valued nondiagonal solution in the $q=4$ model. It appears that the lack of the zero replicas limit is also present in the interacting case. The solutions are plotted on the Fig.3. Note that in the IR region the diagonal and nondiagonal part exhibit similar behavior up to a numerical factor, and the absolute value of that factor approaches to $1$ as $M$ decreases. We also argue that these solutions probably can be analytically constructed in terms of the $1/M$ expansion, which we will investigate in the future work.

- 3. We have shown that the solutions, that we have constructed in the $q=2$ case, are suppressed by the diagonal saddle in the replica path integral for $M>1$ (however, they can dominate in the replica partition function in the $0<M<1$ case). In the $q=4$ SYK the replica-nondiagonal saddles are also subleading for $M>1$ . The fact that nondiagonal saddle points are suppressed at integer $M$ is in agreement with the statement that the SYK partition function is self-averaging at large $N$ [12, 17, 26, 40, 19], as verified by exact diagonalization numerics.

Second, we have studied the analytic nondiagonal solutions in the strong coupling limit $\beta J\gg 1$ . We focused on the class of solutions with the time dependence given by the conformal propagator, and the replica dependence given by a Parisi matrix. The key findings are the following.

- 4. We were able to obtain solutions in the $M\to 0$ limit, using the Parisi ansatz analytic continuation. We have obtained the nondiagonal replica-symmetric solutions, and the solutions with one-step replica symmetry breaking. Meanwhile, the findings of the previous part suggest that these solutions have no well-defined UV completion at $M=0$ , and therefore seem to have no influence on the thermodynamics of SYK at finite coupling. Nevertheless, we calculated the regularized free energy on the solutions. Among them there are some that have global minimum regularized free energy value smaller than the replica-diagonal free energy. We have also checked that at finite $M$ the replica-symmetric solution dominates over the diagonal saddle in the strong coupling limit for $q=4$ and $q=2$ .

- 5. We have illustrated on an $M=2$ example that the extended reparametrization symmetry in the IR limit has interesting consequences, since it can be used to obtain solutions that have spin-glass-like dynamics for a finite amount of time. Another solution that can be obtained using reparametrizations is related by analytic continuation to the purification of the replica-diagonal SYK by the thermofield double.

An important technical question that we left unattended in this work is the problem of stability of the replica-nondiagonal solutions that we have obtained in the interacting $q=4$ model. The numerical solutions of the exact saddle point equations appeared to be stable to small enough fluctuations in the initial condition. As far as the factorized solutions in the strong coupling regime are concerned, the following comments can be made. We can say that the replica-diagonal solution is stable with respect to the replica-diagonal fluctuations of the field $G(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})$ , because the quadratic part of the action is determined by the ladder kernel and it has non-negative eigenvalues [3]. The numerical investigations of [21, 24] confirm that there is no instability to general fluctuations of the replica-diagonal saddle point. Since the time dependence of the factorized solutions is the same, we can expect that they also would be stable with respect to the replica-diagonal fluctuations. However, we also can expect that some of the solutions discussed in the section 6 can be unstable to general fluctuations, because they are defined by pairs of complex saddles, and one would need to take into account fluctuations around both saddles for every solution. It could also be instructive to consider other solutions with several steps or continuous replica symmetry breaking to verify these observations. We leave these questions for the future study.

It is also important to clarify the role of the replica-nondiagonal solutions obtained in the present paper in regards to the previous results about replica-nondiagonality in SYK obtained in the literature. As was mentioned in the introduction, the papers [1, 20, 21, 23, 24, 22] studied the question of the spin glass phase in SY and SYK models, and they argue against the existence of such a phase in fermionic models (but they do not rule out replica-nondiagonal solutions conclusively in general). The exact replica-nondiagonal solutions, constructed in the present work in sections 3 and 4 are time dependent (so do not generally describe glassy physics), and, more importantly, are always subleading in the replica path integral at $M>1$ . Therefore, they do not introduce new phases, but remain a small nonperturbative effect within the $1/N$ expansion of the partition function and some annealed correlators, see Appendix C.

The second class of solutions, that we study in this paper, is restricted to the IR limit of the SYK model. We treat the IR limit of SYK as essentially a low-energy effective field theory with a UV cutoff, and we found nontrivial phase structure in this EFT by studying the regularized free energy. The fact that we have not found any replica-nondiagonal saddles, contributing to the free energy after the zero replicas limit beyond the IR limit, hints that the phase structure of an EFT does not generally match the phase structure of the UV completion (see also discussion in the end of sec.5.2). It is worth noting that the effect of destruction of conformal replica-nondiagonal saddle points by the UV corrections was encountered by authors of [26] in the two-replica case. They explicitly show that the leading UV-correction to the replica-nondiagonal conformal saddle point of the spectral form factor introduces an instability to the contribution of this solution to the path integral. We can expect that at least some of our solutions in the $M\to 0$ limit suffer from the same effect beyond the strong coupling limit.

Let us note that the solutions that we have constructed can be interesting in the following aspects.

- (i) We have shown that the annealed quantites, which would require a finite number of replicas, do have nontrivial repica-nondiagonal saddle points, but they are subleading in the replica partition function. In the case of $M=2$ and complex-valued $\beta$ it is shown that non-trivial saddles can become dominant and are crucial for the quantum dynamics of black holes in the work [17, 26]. Therefore, an interesting problem is to study the counterparts of our saddles in the spectral form-factor, and to see if they can be responsible for the long-time behavior of this quantity.

- (ii) The factorized solutions, which we discussed, also have the emergent conformal symmetry in the strong coupling regime, which suggests the applicability of the holographic description in some sense as well. At finite replica number this would suggest that we need some kind of asymptotically AdS2 space with multiple boundaries. However, we are not aware of such solutions except for the AdS2 itself, which we connected in the section 7.2 to the $M=2$ solution. It would be interesting to find holographic duals to other replica structures.

### A.1 Definition

A symmetric $M\times M$ matrix $Q$ is called the Parisi matrix if it is defined in the following way. The Parisi matrix is associated with a tree

$$ \mathfrak{T}=\mathfrak{T}(r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}...r_{l}) $$

characterized by the set $\{r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}...r_{l}\}$ satisfying

$$ r_{1}\cdot r_{2}...r_{l}=M $$

Note that here the order of $r_{i}$ is important. From this set of numbers one constructs a set of number

$$ \mathfrak{D}_{\mathfrak{T}}=\mathfrak{D}_{\mathfrak{T}}(m_{1},m_{2},r_{3}...m_{l},M), $$

where $m_{i},i=1,...l$ are

$$ m_{i}=\prod_{j=1}^{i-1}r_{j}. $$

As follows from (244) the number $r_{i},m_{i}$ and $m_{i+1}$ are related as

$$ m_{i+1}=m_{i}\cdot r_{i},\,\,\,\,\,i=1,...l-1,\,\,\,\,\,M=m_{l}\cdot r_{l}. $$

The numbers $\{r_{l},...r_{1}\}$ characterize the ramifications in the given tree and $\{m_{l},...m_{1}\}$ , $m_{1}=1$ characterize the thickness of branches corresponding to the same tree, see Fig.11. $l$ is a number of branch points1212 12 One can repeat the the above description of the tree in other words: each tree is characterized by dividing the elements of M into $r_{l}$ groups with $m_{l}$ elements in each, i.e.

$$ M=r_{l}\cdot m_{l}. $$

(246) Then we divide $m_{l}$ elements on $r_{l-1}$ groups with $m_{l-1}$ elements in each, i.e.

(247) and so on. On the last step we left with $r_{1}$ elementary elements, i.e dim $r_{1}=1$ .. We call the number $l$ the rank of the Parisi matrix.

#### Lemma.

The space of Parisi matrices with fixed tree $\mathfrak{T}\{r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}...r_{l}\}$ is an algebra under both regular and Hadamard matrix products.

Proof. The closeness under the Hadamard product is obvious. For the direct matrix product this follows from representation (255) and the following properties (260) of $\mathcal{I}_{m_{i}}$ matrices corresponding to the same tree. Indeed we define the two Parisi matrices of the rank $l$ ( $a_{l+1}=0$ ):

$$ \displaystyle A=\sum_{i=1,\,\,m_{i}\in\mathfrak{T}}^{l}\,a_{i}(\mathcal{I}_{m_{i+1}}-\mathcal{I}_{m_{i}})+q_{0}\mathcal{I}_{1}\,; \displaystyle B=\sum_{i=1,\,\,m_{i}\in\mathfrak{T}}^{l}\,b_{i}(\mathcal{I}_{m_{i+1}}-\mathcal{I}_{m_{i}})+b_{0}\mathcal{I}_{1}\,. $$

We want to calculate their product, which we denote as

$$ W=A\cdot B\,. $$

We proceed as follows:

$$ \displaystyle W=a_{0}b_{0}\mathcal{I}_{1}+\sum_{i}(b_{0}a_{i}+a_{0}b_{i})(\mathcal{I}_{m_{i+1}}-\mathcal{I}_{m_{i}})+\text{four terms}\,. $$

The four terms come from the multiplication of two brackets between each other. Let us evaluate carefully each term using the relation (260). The first term gives

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{T}_{1}:=\sum_{i}\sum_{j}a_{i}b_{j}\mathcal{I}_{m_{i+1}}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}=\sum_{j}\sum_{i<j}a_{i}b_{j}m_{i+1}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}+\sum_{j}a_{j}b_{j}m_{j+1}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}+\sum_{j}\sum_{i>j}a_{i}b_{j}m_{j+1}\mathcal{I}_{m_{i+1}} \displaystyle=\sum_{j}\sum_{i<j}(a_{i}b_{j}+a_{j}b_{i})m_{i+1}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}+\sum_{j}a_{j}b_{j}m_{j+1}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}\,. $$

The second term yields

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{T}_{2}:=-\sum_{i}\sum_{j}a_{i}b_{j}\mathcal{I}_{m_{i}}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}=-\sum_{j}\sum_{i<j+1}a_{i}b_{j}m_{i}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}-\sum_{j}a_{j+1}b_{j}m_{j+1}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}-\sum_{j}\sum_{i>j+1}a_{i}b_{j}m_{j+1}\mathcal{I}_{m_{i}} \displaystyle\!\!\!\!\!\!=-\sum_{j}\sum_{i<j}a_{i}b_{j}m_{i}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}-\sum_{j}a_{j}b_{j}m_{j}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}-\sum_{j}\sum_{i<j}a_{j}b_{i}m_{i+1}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}}\,. $$

We relabeled some summation indices and canceled two terms here. The third term can be obtained from $T_{2}$ by making the replacement $a\leftrightarrow b$ :

$$ \mathrm{T}_{3}:=-\sum_{i}\sum_{j}a_{i}b_{j}\mathcal{I}_{m_{i}+1}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}}=-\sum_{j}\sum_{i<j}b_{i}a_{j}m_{i}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}-\sum_{j=i}a_{j}b_{j}m_{j}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}-\sum_{j}\sum_{i<j}b_{j}a_{i}m_{i+1}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}}\,. $$

The fourth term yields:

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{T}_{4}: \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{i}\sum_{j}a_{i}b_{j}\mathcal{I}_{m_{i}}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}}=\sum_{j}\sum_{i<j}a_{i}b_{j}m_{i}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}}+\sum_{j=i}a_{j}b_{j}m_{j}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}}+\sum_{j}\sum_{i<j}a_{j}b_{i}m_{i}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{j}\sum_{i<j}(a_{i}b_{j}+a_{j}b_{i})m_{i}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}}+\sum_{j=i}a_{j}b_{j}m_{j}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}} $$

where we again relabeled the indices in the last term. Therefore, we have presented the four terms as a linear combination of the $\mathcal{I}$ -matrices, more specifically

$$ \text{four terms}=\sum_{j}(U_{j}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}+V_{j}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}})\,. $$

As it will become clear below, this is already proves the lemma. Let us write down the $U$ and $V$ explicitly:

$$ \displaystyle U_{j}=\sum_{i<j}(a_{i}b_{j}+b_{i}a_{j})(m_{i+1}-m_{i})+a_{j}b_{j}(m_{j+1}-2m_{j})\,. \displaystyle V_{j}=-\sum_{i<j}(a_{i}b_{j}+b_{i}a_{j})(m_{i+1}-m_{i})+a_{j}b_{j}m_{j}\,. $$

As we see, there is a difference between the two:

$$ D_{j}:=U_{j}+V_{j}=a_{j}b_{j}(m_{j+1}-m_{j})\,, $$

and therefore in $W$ there is a rogue term

$$ \sum_{j}D_{j}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}} $$

However, we can deal with it using a trivial formula:

$$ \mathcal{I}_{m_{k}}=\mathcal{I}_{1}+\sum_{j<k}(\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}-\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}})\,. $$

Thus, we can write the term as follows:

$$ \sum_{i}D_{i}\mathcal{I}_{m_{i+1}}=\sum_{i}D_{i}\mathcal{I}_{1}+\sum_{i}\sum_{j<i+1}D_{i}(\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}-\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}})=\sum_{i}D_{i}\mathcal{I}_{1}+\sum_{j}\sum_{i>j-1}D_{i}(\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}-\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}})\,. $$

Therefore, the lemma is proved. We obtain that $W$ is a Parisi matrix

$$ W=\sum_{j}w_{j}(\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}-\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}})+w_{0}\mathcal{I}_{1}\,, $$

where its parameters are given by

$$ \displaystyle w_{0} \displaystyle= \displaystyle a_{0}b_{0}+\sum_{j}a_{j}b_{j}(m_{j+1}-m_{j}); \displaystyle w_{j} \displaystyle= \displaystyle b_{0}a_{j}+a_{0}b_{j}+\sum_{i<j}(a_{i}b_{j}+b_{i}a_{j})(m_{i+1}-m_{i})-a_{j}b_{j}m_{j}+\sum_{i>j-1}a_{i}b_{i}(m_{i+1}-m_{i}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle b_{0}a_{j}+a_{0}b_{j}+\sum_{i<j}(a_{i}b_{j}+b_{i}a_{j})(m_{i+1}-m_{i})-a_{j}b_{j}m_{j}+\sum_{i>j}a_{i}b_{i}(m_{i+1}-m_{i}) \displaystyle+ \displaystyle a_{j}b_{j}(m_{j+1}-m_{j})\,. $$

### A.4 Determinant of the Parisi matrix

The eigenvalues of the Parisi matrix $Q$ are given by the formulae [41]

$$ \displaystyle\lambda_{0} \displaystyle= \displaystyle q_{0}-q_{1} \displaystyle\lambda_{i} \displaystyle= \displaystyle q_{0}-q_{1}+\sum_{j=1}^{i}(q_{j}-q_{j+1})m_{j},\,\,\,\,\,\,i=1,2,...,l-1 \displaystyle\lambda_{l} \displaystyle= \displaystyle q_{0}-q_{1}+\sum_{j=1}^{l-1}(q_{j}-q_{j+1})m_{j}+q_{l}m_{l}. $$

Throughout the paper we compute $\log\det Q$ for different Parisi matrices both at finite and zero $M$ . We illustrate the calculation for $l=1$ and present the result for general $l$ .

In the case of $l=1$ , the determinant for arbitrary $M$ reads:

$$ \det Q=(q_{0}-q_{1})^{M-1}(q_{0}+(M-1)q_{1})\,. $$

For the logarithm we write

$$ \displaystyle\log\det Q=(M-1)\log(q_{0}-q_{1})+\log(q_{0}-q_{1})+\log\left(1+\frac{Mq_{1}}{q_{0}-q_{1}}\right) \displaystyle=M\log(q_{0}-q_{1})+\log\left(1+\frac{Mq_{1}}{q_{0}-q_{1}}\right)\,. $$

Taking the limit $M\to 0$ , we arrive at the expression

$$ \lim_{M\to 0}\frac{1}{M}\log\det Q=\log(q_{0}-q_{1})+\frac{q_{1}}{q_{0}-q_{1}}\,. $$

The cases of higher $l$ can be calculated analogously. The main idea is to extract the part from the lowest degree bracket which is the same as the next degree bracket, which will always be of the odd degree and carry a singular contribution.

For arbitrary $l$ we obtain the expression

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{M\to 0}\frac{1}{M}\log\det Q \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\log(q_{0}-q_{1})+\sum_{i=2}^{l-1}\frac{1}{2^{i}}\log(q_{0}+\sum_{m=0}^{i-1}2^{m}q_{m+2}-2^{i}q_{i+1}) \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2^{k-1}}\log(q_{0}+\sum_{m=0}^{l-1}2^{m}q_{m+2}-2^{l}q_{l})+\frac{1}{2}\frac{q_{l}}{q_{0}+\sum_{m=0}^{l-1}2^{m}q_{m+2}-2^{l}q_{l}}\,. $$

We start with the on-shell action for the path integral (6) at finite $M$ :

$$ \frac{2}{N}S_{M}=-\text{Tr}\log\left(\delta_{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\tau}-\hat{\Sigma}_{\alpha\beta}\right)+\int_{0}^{\beta}\int_{0}^{\beta}d\tau_{1}d\tau_{2}\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\left(G_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})-\frac{J^{2}}{q}G_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})^{q}\right)\Big|_{\text{on-shell}}\,. $$

where the determinant is taken over the replica indices. We denote the polynomial term as

$$ \mathfrak{s}_{2}=\left(1-\frac{1}{q}\right)J^{2}\int_{0}^{\beta}\int_{0}^{\beta}d\tau_{1}d\tau_{2}\sum_{\alpha,\beta}G_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})^{q}\Big|_{\text{on-shell}}\,. $$

#### Replica-symmetric ansatz.

In this case we have two dynamical variables $G_{0,1}$ (and corresponding $\Sigma_{0,1}(\tau)=J^{2}G_{0,1}^{q-1}(\tau)$ ). To evauate the Pfaffian term in the frequency space we use the formula for the determinant of a Parisi matrix (284) for every frequency:

$$ \log\det\left(\delta_{\alpha\beta}+\frac{\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}(\omega)}{i\omega}\right)=M\log\left(1+\frac{\Sigma_{0}(\omega)}{i\omega}-\frac{\Sigma_{1}(\omega)}{i\omega}\right)+\log\left(1+M\frac{\Sigma_{1}(\omega)}{i\omega+\Sigma_{0}(\omega)-\Sigma_{1}(\omega)}\right)\,. $$

## Appendix C Observables and disorder: annealed vs quenched

Having found replica-nondiagonal solutions in $q=2$ and $q=4$ SYK models, it is appropriate to discuss which observables will be affected by these saddle points. For this purpose, it is useful to review the two types of correlation functions, which one can consider in a disordered model.

First, let us remind that the Lagrangian of the SYK model is given by [7, 3, 4]

$$ L[\psi,{\bf j}]=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}\psi_{i}\frac{d}{d\tau}\psi_{i}-\frac{i^{q/2}}{q!}\sum_{i_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{q}}j_{i_{1}i_{2}\dots\char 16\relax_{q}}\psi_{i_{1}}\psi_{i_{2}}\dots\psi_{i_{q}}\,, $$

which is used to construct the generating functional of SYK correlation functions for a fixed realization of disorder ${\bf j}=\{j_{i_{1}i_{2}\dots\char 16\relax_{q}}\}$ :

$$ Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;\eta)=\int D\psi\exp\left[-\int_{0}^{\beta}d\tau L[\psi,{\bf j}]+\int_{0}^{\beta}\eta_{i}(\tau)\psi_{i}(\tau)d\tau\right]\,. $$

Here we have introduced the fermionic sources $\eta_{i}(\tau)$ . The correlation functions in a fixed realization of disorder are defined as usual:

$$ \langle\psi_{i_{1}}(\tau_{1})\dots\psi_{i_{k}}(\tau_{k})\rangle_{{\bf j}}=\frac{1}{Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;0)}\frac{1}{k!}\left.\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta_{i_{1}}(\tau_{1})}\dots\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta_{i_{k}}(\tau_{k})}Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;\eta)\right|_{\eta=0}\,. $$

As a final preliminary remark, the average over the disorder of a function $f({\bf j})$ is performed by taking the integral

$$ \overline{f({\bf j})}=\int d{\bf j}\ P({\bf j})f({\bf j})\,, $$

where the Gaussian distribution $P({\bf j})$ is given by (2).

### C.1 Quenched quantities

In the quenched quantities the disorder averaging is performed on the last step. The quenched correlators are defined as

$$ \overline{\langle\psi_{i_{1}}(\tau_{1})\dots\psi_{i_{k}}(\tau_{k})\rangle}=\overline{\frac{1}{Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;0)}\frac{1}{k!}\left.\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta_{i_{1}}(\tau_{1})}\dots\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta_{i_{k}}(\tau_{k})}Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;\eta)\right|_{\eta=0}}\,. $$

Because the nominator and denominator are averaged together, these quantities require replica trick, and specifically they require taking the limit $M\to 0$ . Below we explicitly derive the representation of the quenched correlators in terms of the bilocal replica field path integral.

#### C.1.1 Replica-diagonal case

We start with the singlet two-point function of fermions in a single copy of SYK1313 13 We also emphasize the $N$ dependence for purposes of the further discussion:

$$ \mathcal{G}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N):=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overline{\langle\psi_{i}(\tau_{1})\psi_{i}(\tau_{2})\rangle}=\frac{1}{2!N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overline{\frac{1}{Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;0)}\left.\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta_{i}(\tau_{1})}\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta_{i}(\tau_{2})}Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;\eta)\right|_{\eta=0}}\,. $$

Now let us derive the expression for $\mathcal{G}$ in terms of the disorder-averaged bilocal replica field path integral. Let us define the bilocal field correlator in the disorder-averaged SYK with $M$ replicas:

$$ \displaystyle\mathfrak{G}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N,M) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int\prod_{\alpha,\beta=1}^{M}DG_{\alpha\beta}D\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}\ \mathrm{e}^{-NS[G_{\alpha\beta},\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}]}G_{MM}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\,. $$

In terms of this quantity, the quenched correlator is written as following:

$$ \mathcal{G}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N)=\lim_{M\to 0}\mathfrak{G}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N,M)\,. $$

Let us sketch the proof. On the first step we take the derivatives in (300) and write the nominator partition function explicitly as the path integral. For the normalizing denominator, we use the following formal identity [29]:

$$ Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;0)^{-1}=\lim_{M\to 0}Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;0)^{M-1}\,. $$

We get (the summation over color indices is implicit)

$$ \mathcal{G}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N)=\frac{1}{N}\overline{\lim_{M\to 0}Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;0)^{M-1}\int D\psi^{M}\ \mathrm{e}^{-S_{\text{SYK}}[{\bf j},\psi^{M}]}\psi_{i}^{M}(\tau_{1})\psi_{i}^{M}(\tau_{2})}\,, $$

where we have assigned a replica index $M$ to fermion fields participating in the last path integral. We can rewrite this as the path integral over $M$ replicas with insertions supported on the $M$ -th replica:

$$ \mathcal{G}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N)=\frac{1}{N}\overline{\lim_{M\to 0}\int\prod_{\alpha=1}^{M}D\psi^{\alpha}\ \mathrm{e}^{-\sum_{\alpha=1}^{M}S_{\text{SYK}}[{\bf j},\psi^{\alpha}]}\psi_{i}^{M}(\tau_{1})\psi_{i}^{M}(\tau_{2})}\,, $$

The averaging over the disorder can be performed in this replica integral in the same way as in the partition function (6). After that, we can rewrite this in terms of the bilocal fields with the fermions integrated out: 1414 14 This identity holds up to some numerical constants which come from the measure [4], which we omit:

$$ \overline{\int\prod_{\alpha^{\prime}=1}^{M}D\psi^{\alpha^{\prime}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-\sum_{\alpha^{\prime}=1}^{M}S_{\text{SYK}}[{\bf j},\psi^{\alpha^{\prime}}]}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\psi_{i}^{M}(\tau_{1})\psi_{i}^{M}(\tau_{2})}=\int\prod_{\alpha,\beta=1}^{M}DG_{\alpha\beta}D\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}\ \mathrm{e}^{-NS[G_{\alpha\beta},\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}]}G_{MM}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\,. $$

Thus, we obtain the formula (302):

$$ \mathcal{G}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N)=\lim_{M\to 0}\int\prod_{\alpha,\beta=1}^{M}DG_{\alpha\beta}D\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}\ \mathrm{e}^{-NS[G_{\alpha\beta},\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}]}G_{MM}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\,. $$

We see that a quenched correlator is expressed in terms of replica correlators in the limit $M\to 0$ . Note that this limit is taken before the thermodynamic limit $N\to\infty$ .

#### C.1.2 Replica-offdiagonal case

A common diagonostic of the spin glass physics is the quenched replica-offdiagonal correlator [24, 6, 1, 20, 35, 28, 21, 34]. Let us start with the two replicas $\alpha$ and $\beta$ of the given system. The offdiagonal quenched correlator is defined as

$$ \mathcal{G}_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N):=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overline{\langle\psi_{i}^{\alpha}(\tau_{1})\psi^{\beta}_{i}(\tau_{2})\rangle}=\frac{1}{2!N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overline{\frac{1}{Z^{(2)}_{{\bf j}}(\beta;0)}\left.\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta^{\alpha}_{i}(\tau_{1})}\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta^{\beta}_{i}(\tau_{2})}Z_{{\bf j}}^{(2)}(\beta;\eta^{\alpha},\eta^{\beta})\right|_{\eta=0}}\,. $$

Here $Z^{(2)}$ is the two-replica partition function. If the two replicas are independent, then $Z^{(2)}_{\bf j}(\beta;\eta^{\alpha},\eta^{\beta})=Z_{\bf j}(\beta;\eta^{\alpha})Z_{\bf j}(\beta;\eta^{\beta})$ and the expression under line can factorizes into product of two one-point functions:

$$ \overline{\frac{1}{Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;0)^{2}}\left.\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta^{\alpha}_{i}(\tau_{1})}\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta^{\beta}_{i}(\tau_{2})}Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;\eta^{\alpha})Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;\eta^{\beta})\right|_{\eta=0}}=\overline{\langle\psi_{i}^{\alpha}(\tau_{1})\rangle\langle\psi_{i}^{\beta}(\tau_{1})\rangle}\,. $$

In the fermionic theory, like SYK, the one-point functions vanish, which, assuming $N$ is finite, gives that in total $\mathcal{G}_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})=0$ 1515 15 This argument does not generally work in the thermodynamic limit $N\to\infty$ .. This is a general argument that is often presented to support the absense of spin glass phase in fermionic models such as variations of SY and SYK [24, 1, 20, 35, 21].

Let us now see what this tells us about the replica structure of the $G$ , $\Sigma$ saddle points. We again define the replica bilocal field correlator

$$ \displaystyle\mathfrak{G}_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N,M) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int\prod_{\alpha,\beta=1}^{M}DG_{\alpha\beta}D\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}\ \mathrm{e}^{-NS[G_{\alpha\beta},\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}]}G_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\,,\quad\alpha\neq\beta\,. $$

Note that, formally speaking, $\mathfrak{G}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N,M)=\mathfrak{G}_{MM}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N,M)$ (see (301)). Analogously to the diagonal case (302), one can derive the bilocal field representation for the quenched offdiagonal correlator:

$$ \mathcal{G}_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N)=\lim_{M\to 0}\mathfrak{G}_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N,M)\,. $$

The proof goes as follows. Proceeding analogously to the derivation of the expression (302) above, we write

$$ \mathcal{G}_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N)=\frac{1}{N}\overline{\lim_{M\to 0}Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;0)^{M-2}\int D\psi^{\alpha}D\psi^{\beta}\ \mathrm{e}^{-S_{\text{SYK}}[{\bf j},\psi^{\alpha}]-S_{\text{SYK}}[{\bf j},\psi^{\beta}]}\psi_{i}^{\alpha}(\tau_{1})\psi_{i}^{\beta}(\tau_{2})}\,, $$

or in terms of the disorder-averaged replica bilocal field theory we obtain

$$ \mathcal{G}_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N)=\lim_{M\to 0}\int\prod_{\gamma,\delta=1}^{M}DG_{\gamma\delta}D\Sigma_{\gamma\delta}\ \mathrm{e}^{-NS[G_{\gamma\delta},\Sigma_{\gamma\delta}]}G_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\,. $$

This formula gives representation for non-diagonal disorder correlator in terms of the disorder-averaged replica bilocal field theory. We once again see that the quenched correlator is governed by the replica structure in the limit $M\to 0$ .

The replica factorization and vanishing of the fermionic one-point functions at large (but finite) $N$ seems to tell that there should be no replica-nondiagonal saddle points, but in fact this is not conclusive. It is worth noting that the factorization argument holds at finite $N$ , and it does not exclude possible dominant non-diagonal saddle points in the thermodynamic limit $N\to\infty$ . The factorization adds a nontrivial nonperturbative constraint on the full $1/N$ expansion of the right hand side of (311). In particular, at some orders of $1/N$ one expects replica-nondiagonal contributions in perturbations even over the replica-diagonal saddle [35, 16, 4]. The factorization in the fermionic case implies that all such perturbative corrections should resum to zero, together with any nonperturbative corrections (that come e.g. from subleading saddles). Of course, with only finite amount of the asymptotic $1/N$ series taken into account, one does not expect zero. This will be more relevant to our results in the case of annealed correlators.

### C.2 Annealed quantities

The quantities, which are obtained by performing annealed averaging, treat the disorder on equal footing with other microscopic degrees of freedom of the model. In the general case, one can also consider annealed quantities that deal with $M$ copies of the initial model by construction. The simplest example is the replica partition function $\overline{Z(\beta)^{M}}$ , which we consider throughout the paper, taken with an integer $M$ . As we show in sections 3 and 4, there are nontrivial exact replica-nondiagonal saddle points, contributing to this quantity in case of a finite replica number. We also show that these saddle points are suppressed at large $N$ , giving nonperturbative contributions to the $1/N$ -expansion that are suppressed exponentially like $\mathrm{e}^{-NS}$ .

Another closely related example of an annealed quantity is the spectral form factor $\frac{1}{\overline{Z(\beta)^{2}}}\overline{Z(\beta+iT)Z(\beta-iT)}$ , which is essential in studies of quantum chaos and quantum gravity [17, 19, 26]. The study of replica-nondiagonal saddle points of this and related quantities is the topic of the future work.

Below we consider the annealed correlators. The annealed correlation functions are computed by performing the average over the disorder in the normalization and in the nominator of (297) separately.

#### C.2.1 Single-replica correlators

If the fields all belong to the same one replica of the theory initially, the correlator is written

$$ \langle\psi_{i_{1}}(\tau_{1})\dots\psi_{i_{k}}(\tau_{k})\rangle_{\text{annealed}}=\frac{1}{\overline{Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;0)}}\frac{1}{k!}\left.\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta_{i_{1}}(\tau_{1})}\dots\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta_{i_{k}}(\tau_{k})}\overline{Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;\eta)}\right|_{\eta=0}\,. $$

The integral over the disorder is a straightforward Gaussian integral in both nominator and denominator and can be taken right away. The single-replica annealed correlators do not have any replica structure.

In terms of the bilocal fields $G$ , $\Sigma$ the annealed two-point function is written as

$$ \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\langle\psi_{i}(\tau_{1})\psi_{i}(\tau_{2})\rangle_{\text{annealed}}=\frac{\int DGD\Sigma\ \mathrm{e}^{-NS[G,\Sigma]}G(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})}{\int DGD\Sigma\ \mathrm{e}^{-NS[G,\Sigma]}}\,. $$

#### C.2.2 Replica-offdiagonal correlators

Finally, one can consider the replica-offdiagonal annealed correlators of the form

$$ \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\langle\psi_{i}^{\alpha}(\tau_{1})\psi^{\beta}_{i}(\tau_{2})\rangle_{\text{annealed}}=\frac{1}{2!N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\overline{Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;0)^{2}}}\left.\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta^{\alpha}_{i}(\tau_{1})}\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta^{\beta}_{i}(\tau_{2})}\overline{Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;\eta^{\alpha})Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;\eta^{\beta})}\right|_{\eta=0}\,. $$

#### Factorization.

Note that this correlator does not factorize into product of one-point functions due to the fact that disorder averaging introduces interaction between replicas. However, the fermionic path integral still factorizes at finite $N$ . Taking the derivatives in the right hand side of (316), one obtains under the averaging line the product of two copies of

$$ \int D\psi\ \mathrm{e}^{-S_{\text{SYK}}[{\bf j},\psi]}\,. $$

This is zero at finite $N$ due to parity, and therefore also nullifies the correlator (316).

#### Bilocal field representation and $1/N$ -expansion.

In terms of the bilocal replica fields, the correlator (316) reads

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\langle\psi_{i}^{\alpha}(\tau_{1})\psi^{\beta}_{i}(\tau_{2})\rangle_{\text{annealed}} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{\overline{Z(\beta)^{2}}}\mathfrak{G}_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N,2) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{\int\prod_{\gamma,\delta=1}^{2}DG_{\gamma\delta}D\Sigma_{\gamma\delta}\ \mathrm{e}^{-NS[G_{\gamma\delta},\Sigma_{\gamma\delta}]}G_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})}{\int\prod_{\gamma,\delta=1}^{2}DG_{\gamma\delta}D\Sigma_{\gamma\delta}\ \mathrm{e}^{-NS[G_{\gamma\delta},\Sigma_{\gamma\delta}]}}\,, $$

where $M=2$ . Note that there is a normalization factor, unlike the quenched case. This correlator requires two replicas, and can detect replica-nondiagonal saddle points, obtained in sections 3 and 4. We have shown that those saddle points are suppressed at large $N$ , thus their effect can only appear at finite $N$ .

However, at finite $N$ the factorization of the fermionic path integral dictates that (316) exactly should be zero. But here one can repeat the same arguments as in the disorder case in the end of sec.C.1.2. We can also expect that at finite $N$ the replica-nondiagonal saddle points may give a nonperturbatively small contribution to annealed $4$ - and higher-point nondiagonal correlators.
